CPP at 60, 65 or 70: chart the timing trade-off and the income bridge

Compare monthly CPP age adjustments, cumulative receipts and discounted payment timing with four graphics and a clearly stated common benefit assumption.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore CPP start-age adjustments

Interactive planning lab

Monthly pension · start 65$1,000
Monthly pension · start 70$1,420

Simplified CPP age-adjustment illustration, not a personal benefit estimate. The same assumed age-65 entitlement is held fixed across start ages. All amounts use constant purchasing-power dollars with no tax, benefit interactions or further contribution accrual. A full payment year runs from one birthday to the next, with payments at month-end. Discounted receipts are valued at age 60 using the selected real rate. Survival probabilities, survivor benefits and QPP rules are excluded.

The central idea

A later start trades early cash flow for a larger payment later. Compare that trade-off with the cost of funding the waiting period and the household’s other needs.

01

Separate the age adjustment from the entitlement estimate

The Government of Canada’s CPP start-age guidance states that the standard start age is 65, with starts available from 60 to 70. Before 65, the monthly amount is reduced by 0.6% for each month early. After 65, it increases by 0.7% for each month delayed, through age 70.

The first chart applies those factors to one common assumed age-65 entitlement. At the default CAD 1,000 per month, the illustrative payments are CAD 640 at 60, CAD 1,000 at 65 and CAD 1,420 at 70. The CAD 1,000 input is neither an official maximum nor an average payment.

A personal CPP estimate also depends on the contribution record and applicable calculation rules. Working longer or changing future contributions can change that underlying entitlement. This tool freezes the entitlement to isolate the age adjustment. It does not retrieve a contribution history or calculate the pension that a particular person will receive.

02

Read the cash-flow head start

The cumulative chart counts the payments received by each birthday. At the chosen starting birthday, cumulative receipts are zero; the following birthday includes twelve month-end payments. The age axis begins at 60 so the years relevant to the comparison remain visible.

Starting at 65 provides five years of payments before a start at 70 begins. Under the default assumption, that head start is CAD 60,000 in constant purchasing-power dollars. After 70, the later-start case receives CAD 420 more each month. It gradually makes up the difference if the person continues receiving payments.

Ignoring discounting, tax and all other effects, the continuous arithmetic crossover is about age 81.9 for 65 versus 70. With month-end payments, the first crossover is at the 143rd payment after age 70. This is a conditional receipt calculation. It does not establish the age a person will live to or recommend waiting until 70.

03

Account for when the money arrives

A dollar available sooner and a dollar received decades later have different timing. The present-value bars discount each monthly payment back to age 60 using the selected real annual rate, converted to an equivalent monthly rate.

All payments in the illustration are expressed in constant purchasing-power dollars. The discount rate must therefore also be real. Using a nominal investment return against these real cash flows would mix measurement bases. The tool does not separately forecast CPI or reproduce actual annual CPP indexation.

A positive discount rate gives more weight to earlier payments. The matrix compares start-at-70 receipts with start-at-65 receipts over several final ages and discount rates. Each signed cell is a present-value difference at age 60. A negative cell favors the earlier receipts under that calculation; a positive cell favors the later receipts. There is no probability attached to a cell.

04

Plan the years before the pension starts

The charts count CPP receipts only. They do not deduct the resources needed to pay household expenses while waiting. If employment, other pensions or savings must cover that period, write down the annual shortfalls and identify their funding sources.

A person who uses an investment portfolio for the bridge may make larger withdrawals before CPP starts. The portfolio’s return sequence, tax cost and remaining flexibility then matter. The sequence-risk guide explains why the same average investment return can produce different results when withdrawals occur.

Conversely, a household with sufficient income from elsewhere may value the larger later monthly payment differently from one with immediate cash needs. A simple cumulative-payment crossover cannot represent all those circumstances. Compare a full household cash-flow plan alongside the receipt chart.

05

Treat longevity and benefit interactions separately

Every plotted receipt assumes the person is alive to receive it. The model applies no survival probabilities and computes no expected present value. A comparison through age 95 is an assumption about the payment horizon, rather than a prediction or a statement about population life expectancy.

Taxes, income-tested benefits, survivor benefits, disability-related provisions, future contributions and QPP rules are outside the tool. These can affect an actual decision. A household review should also consider health, a spouse or partner’s cash flows, debt costs, flexibility and the consequence of living longer than initially planned.

Use an up-to-date personal estimate and verify the applicable rules before implementing a start date. Keep the entitlement estimate, age adjustment, payment timing and bridge funding as distinct inputs. The four charts make one part of that decision visible while leaving room for the circumstances that a receipt-only model cannot resolve.
